definition: An iterator is an object that enables a programmer to traverse a container, particularly lists.
details: An iterator is an object that enables a programmer to traverse a container, particularly lists. Various types of iterators are capable of accessing the data elements of a container in a sequential manner.

explainer.lead: An iterator is an object that gives a programmer sequential access to each item of a collection in order. It matters because it hides a collection's internal structure while exposing its elements as a sequence.

tiers.eli5: Like a bookmark that moves down a list one page at a time, handing you each item without showing how the list is stored.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use iterators to loop over collections without touching internal layout; a common pitfall is that some iterators are tightly coupled to their collection, so changing the collection during traversal can break correctness.
tiers.paperLevel: An object providing element access and element traversal, changing internal state to reach the next element, with creation and initialization to a first element and an indication of whether all elements have been traversed. Collections may supply multiple iterators with different orders, such as forwards and backwards; behavior is similar to a database cursor and dates to CLU in 1974.

explainer.example: A list exposes a forward iterator that returns the first element, then each next element, until it signals traversal is complete.
